Random effects with lme4 bar syntax

Source: vignettes/random-effects.Rmd
random-effects.Rmd
library(tulpaObs)

When a grouping factor needs a random effect

Surveys come with structure that is not a covariate of interest. Sites fall into clusters, observers differ in how hard they look, regions sit under their own unmeasured baseline. You could enter the grouping factor as a fixed effect, one coefficient per level, and for a handful of levels that is fine. With thirty observers or two hundred site clusters it stops being fine: each level gets its own intercept estimated from its own sparse data, the levels with little data get wild estimates, and nothing ties them together.

A random effect ties them together. Instead of estimating each level freely, you assume the level effects are draws from a common distribution, bg∼N(0,σ2)b_g \sim N(0, \sigma^2), and estimate the spread σ\sigma. A level with plenty of data keeps most of its own signal; a level with little data is pulled toward the population mean. The model spends one parameter on the spread rather than one per level, and the per-level estimates borrow strength from each other. This is the difference between asking “what is this observer’s intercept” and “how much do observers vary, and where does this one sit”.

The honest question to ask first is which one you want. If the grouping factor has a few levels and each is interesting in its own right (three treatment arms, two field protocols), a fixed effect names them and is the right tool. If it has many exchangeable levels and you care about the variance more than any single level, a random effect is the right tool. tulpaObs writes random effects the way lme4 does, inside the formula, with a bar.

The pull toward the mean is called shrinkage, and it is the feature, not a side effect. A cluster surveyed once contributes one noisy observation; on its own that observation would give a wild intercept. The random effect treats it as a draw from the population and reports an estimate close to the population mean, because the data give little reason to move it. A cluster surveyed two hundred times anchors its own estimate, because its data dominate the prior. The amount of shrinkage is set by the data, not chosen: it falls out of the ratio between within-group noise and the estimated between-group variance σ2\sigma^2. This is also why a random effect reports honest uncertainty. A fixed effect with one observation per level claims a precise intercept it has no right to; the random effect admits it is mostly guessing the mean.

Bar syntax

A random-effect term is (<effects> | <grouping factor>). The left side says which coefficients vary by group; the right side names the grouping factor (a factor in your data frame). The double bar || drops the correlation between a group’s intercept and its slopes. The supported forms:

Form Meaning
(1 | g) random intercept per level of g
(x | g) random intercept and slope on x, correlated
(1 + x | g) the same, written explicitly
(x || g) random intercept and slope, uncorrelated
(1 + x || g) the same, written explicitly
(0 + x | g) random slope on x, no group intercept
(1 | g:h) random intercept for each crossed combination of g and h
(1 | g/h) nested: a g intercept plus an h-within-g intercept

A term enters whichever linear predictor its formula sits in. Put (1 | g) in the occupancy formula and it varies occupancy by group; put it in the detection formula and it varies detection by group. The process membership comes from the formula, not from a separate argument.

Under the hood tulpaObs rewrites the bars into re() calls on the formula tree before parsing, so there is one parser and one term type. You never call re() yourself; the bar is the surface you type.

A random intercept under Laplace

Start with the simplest case: occupancy varies by a site cluster. We simulate thirty clusters of twenty-five sites each, give each cluster its own intercept drawn from N(0,0.92)N(0, 0.9^2), and add one site covariate x. Detection is constant at about 0.45 across six visits.

sim_re <- function(seed = 101, ng = 30L, per = 25L, J = 6L,
                   b0 = 0.3, b1 = -0.6, sigma = 0.9, p = 0.45) {
  set.seed(seed)
  N <- ng * per
  g <- rep(seq_len(ng), each = per)
  x <- rnorm(N)
  b_true <- rnorm(ng, 0, sigma)               # the per-cluster intercepts
  z <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(b0 + b1 * x + b_true[g]))
  y <- matrix(0L, N, J)
  for (i in seq_len(N)) y[i, ] <- rbinom(J, 1, z[i] * p)
  list(y = y, d = data.frame(g = factor(g), x = x), b_true = b_true)
}

s <- sim_re()
str(s$d)

The grouping factor g is a factor. Fit occupancy with a fixed slope on x and a random intercept for g. The default method = "laplace" fits the random effect through a variance-component EM; pass verbose = FALSE so the EM does not print its iterations.

fit <- tobs(
  ~ x + (1 | g),
  data      = s$d,
  y         = s$y,
  detection = ~ 1,
  family    = occu(),
  method    = "laplace",
  control   = list(verbose = FALSE)
)

The fixed effects come back from coef() as usual. The occupancy intercept and slope land near the simulated 0.3 and -0.6.

coef(fit, arm = "psi")

The variance component is a hyperparameter in fit$means, named for the group it belongs to. There is one sigma_ entry for the random intercept.

sig_name <- grep("^sigma_", names(fit$means), value = TRUE)
sig_name
c(estimate = fit$means[[sig_name]], truth = 0.9)

ranef() returns the per-group effects (the BLUPs, best linear unbiased predictors) as a data frame with one row per group and term: which grouping factor, which level, which coefficient, the estimate, and its standard error.

re <- ranef(fit)
head(re)
nrow(re)

The point of the random effect is that these per-cluster intercepts track the truth. Plotting the recovered BLUPs against the simulated cluster effects shows the model recovers the cluster-level signal, with the shrinkage that pulls small-data clusters toward zero.

plot(s$b_true, re$estimate, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.5),
     xlab = "true cluster effect", ylab = "estimated BLUP")
abline(0, 1, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
cor(s$b_true, re$estimate)

The EM, the small-cluster bias, and the AGHQ debias

The default Laplace path integrates the random-effect block with a Gaussian approximation at its mode. For binary occupancy data that is the glmer nAGQ = 1 regime: the per-group integral is approximated by a single Gaussian, and at small per-group sample sizes that approximation pulls the estimated variance toward zero. The point estimates and the fixed-effect standard errors are fine; the variance component itself comes out attenuated.

tulpaObs corrects this by default with an adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature pass. After the EM converges it replaces the single-Gaussian per-group integral with a quadrature grid, which captures the curvature the Laplace approximation misses, and re-estimates the variance component. The control is re.aghq (on by default) and n.quad (the number of quadrature nodes, default 9). The fit records what happened in fit$aghq.

fit$aghq$applied
fit$aghq$n_quad

The effect is largest when groups are small. With per-group n=8n = 8 the measured sigma bias runs about 18% under the raw EM and drops to about 4% after the AGHQ pass, matching a NUTS fit. We can see the direction on a single small-cluster dataset by turning the pass off and on.

s8 <- sim_re(seed = 21, ng = 30L, per = 8L, sigma = 0.9)

fit_em <- tobs(~ x + (1 | g), data = s8$d, y = s8$y, detection = ~ 1,
               family = occu(), method = "laplace",
               control = list(re.aghq = FALSE, verbose = FALSE))
fit_aghq <- tobs(~ x + (1 | g), data = s8$d, y = s8$y, detection = ~ 1,
                 family = occu(), method = "laplace",
                 control = list(re.aghq = TRUE, verbose = FALSE))

get_sigma <- function(f) f$means[[grep("^sigma_", names(f$means), value = TRUE)]]
c(truth = 0.9,
  EM    = get_sigma(fit_em),
  AGHQ  = get_sigma(fit_aghq))

The EM estimate sits below the truth; the AGHQ pass corrects it upward. The mechanism is worth one sentence: a single Gaussian centred at the per-group mode underweights the tails of the integral over the group effect, and for binary data that loss falls on the variance, so the estimate shrinks. Adding quadrature nodes samples those tails and recovers the spread. You rarely need to think about this. The default does the right thing, and fit$aghq$applied tells you it ran. The pass applies to one grouping factor on one predictor with random-effect dimension up to 3; outside that (a random effect split across both occupancy and detection, crossed or nested groupings) the fit keeps the EM estimate, and NUTS is available for the full treatment.

Correlated random slopes

A random slope lets the covariate effect vary by group, not just the intercept. (1 + x | g) gives each group its own intercept and its own slope on x, with a correlation between the two estimated as well. We simulate from a known 2×22 \times 2 covariance with a positive intercept-slope correlation.

sim_corr <- function(seed = 402, ng = 40L, per = 25L, J = 6L,
                     b0 = 0.2, b1 = -0.4, p = 0.5,
                     Sigma = matrix(c(0.6, 0.3, 0.3, 0.4), 2, 2)) {
  set.seed(seed)
  N <- ng * per
  g <- rep(seq_len(ng), each = per)
  x <- rnorm(N)
  U <- matrix(rnorm(ng * 2L), ng, 2L) %*% chol(Sigma)   # rows ~ N(0, Sigma)
  eta <- b0 + U[g, 1] + (b1 + U[g, 2]) * x
  z <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(eta))
  y <- matrix(0L, N, J)
  for (i in seq_len(N)) y[i, ] <- rbinom(J, 1, z[i] * p)
  list(y = y, d = data.frame(g = factor(g), x = x), U = U, Sigma = Sigma)
}

sc <- sim_corr()
fit_c <- tobs(~ x + (1 + x | g), data = sc$d, y = sc$y, detection = ~ 1,
              family = occu(), method = "laplace",
              control = list(verbose = FALSE))

The block reports two standard deviations (one for the intercept, one for the slope) and the off-diagonal as a correlation named cor_<g>_.... The true correlation here is 0.3/0.6×0.4≈0.610.3 / \sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4} \approx 0.61.

fit_c$means[grep("^sigma_|^cor_", names(fit_c$means))]

The Laplace correlation is regularized by a default LKJ(η=1.5\eta = 1.5) penalty (re.lkj) on each correlated block. A random-effect correlation is often weakly identified, and unregularized maximum likelihood can pin it against ±1\pm 1. The LKJ penalty pulls a weakly-identified correlation off the boundary toward zero without touching the marginal standard deviations. Set re.lkj = 1 to disable it; for a full posterior treatment of the correlation, use NUTS.

The per-group slopes recover too. The ranef() table now carries both an (Intercept) term and an x term per group.

re_c <- ranef(fit_c)
unique(re_c$term)
b1_hat <- re_c$estimate[re_c$term == "x"]
cor(b1_hat, sc$U[, 2])

The uncorrelated forms (x || g), (1 + x || g), and the slope-only (0 + x | g) fit the same way; they drop the off-diagonal, so you get the standard deviations without a cor_ entry. Use || when you have no reason to expect the intercept and slope deviations to move together, or when the correlation is too weakly informed to estimate.

Crossed and nested grouping

Two grouping factors can apply at once. They are crossed when every level of one can pair with every level of the other (sites visited by any of several observers), and nested when each level of the inner factor belongs to exactly one level of the outer (transects within plots). The bar syntax follows lme4: (1 | g:h) is crossed, (1 | g/h) is nested.

Crossed grouping builds one random intercept for each observed combination of the two factors. We cross eight site groups with six survey rounds and give each combination its own occupancy intercept.

set.seed(55)
ng <- 8L; nh <- 6L; per <- 12L
combos <- expand.grid(g = seq_len(ng), h = seq_len(nh))
N <- nrow(combos) * per
g <- rep(combos$g, each = per); h <- rep(combos$h, each = per)
gh <- interaction(factor(g), factor(h), drop = TRUE)
b_gh <- rnorm(nlevels(gh), 0, 0.8)
x <- rnorm(N)
z <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(0.2 - 0.4 * x + b_gh[gh]))
y <- matrix(0L, N, 6L)
for (i in seq_len(N)) y[i, ] <- rbinom(6L, 1, z[i] * 0.5)
d_cr <- data.frame(g = factor(g), h = factor(h), x = x)

fit_cr <- tobs(~ x + (1 | g:h), data = d_cr, y = y, detection = ~ 1,
               family = occu(), method = "laplace",
               control = list(verbose = FALSE))
nrow(ranef(fit_cr))      # one BLUP per observed g:h combination
coef(fit_cr, arm = "psi")

The crossed term (1 | g:h) collapses to a single interaction factor, so the Laplace path treats it as one grouping factor and the AGHQ debias applies. The nested form (1 | g/h) expands to two terms, an outer g intercept and an inner h-within-g intercept; the EM fits both, and the AGHQ debias steps aside because there is more than one grouping factor. Read the nested variance components as the attenuated EM estimates, or refit under NUTS when the variance partition matters.

A random effect on detection

Detection effort varies by observer. Put the bar in the detection formula and the random effect moves the detection probability instead of occupancy. Here observers each have their own detection intercept, drawn from N(0,0.82)N(0, 0.8^2), while occupancy depends on a site covariate with no random part.

sim_det <- function(seed = 1, N = 400L, J = 6L, ng = 40L,
                    b0 = 0.4, b1 = -0.7, d0 = 0.2, sigma = 0.8) {
  set.seed(seed)
  occ_cov  <- rnorm(N)
  observer <- sample.int(ng, N, replace = TRUE)
  b_obs    <- rnorm(ng, 0, sigma)
  z <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(b0 + b1 * occ_cov))
  p <- plogis(d0 + b_obs[observer])
  y <- matrix(0L, N, J)
  for (i in seq_len(N)) if (z[i] == 1L) y[i, ] <- rbinom(J, 1L, p[i])
  list(y = y, d = data.frame(occ_cov = occ_cov, observer = factor(observer)),
       b_obs = b_obs)
}

sd_re <- sim_det()
fit_d <- tobs(~ occ_cov, detection = ~ (1 | observer), family = occu(),
              data = sd_re$d, y = sd_re$y, method = "laplace",
              control = list(verbose = FALSE))

The variance component now belongs to the detection arm, so it is named for the detection process: sigma_p<t>_ rather than the occupancy sigma_g<t>_. The AGHQ pass records that it ran on the detection arm.

grep("^sigma_", names(fit_d$means), value = TRUE)
fit_d$aghq$arm

The detection arm is harder than the occupancy arm because only occupied sites carry information about detection. A site that is empty tells you nothing about how well the observer detects. The raw EM attenuates the detection-RE variance heavily for that reason (about 70% in the measured sims), and the AGHQ pass on the exact detection marginal restores it to within about 1% with 88-96% fixed-effect interval coverage. The per-group detection BLUPs track the simulated observer effects.

re_d <- ranef(fit_d)
rp <- re_d[re_d$group == "p1", ]
cor(rp$estimate, sd_re$b_obs)

Laplace versus NUTS for random effects

The Laplace path with the AGHQ debias covers the common single-grouping cases: a random intercept or slope on one of the two predictors, with the variance component corrected for the small-cluster bias. NUTS fits every random-effect form and returns the full posterior, including the full posterior of the correlation rather than a regularized point estimate. It is the tool for the forms Laplace declines and for any case where you want draws rather than a Gaussian approximation.

Here is the same random intercept under NUTS. The variance component comes back on the log scale as log_sigma_, and ranef() reconstructs the per-group BLUPs by marginalising over the draws.

fit_n <- tobs(~ x + (1 | g), data = s$d, y = s$y, detection = ~ 1,
              family = occu(), method = "nuts",
              control = list(n.iter = 400, n.warmup = 200, seed = 1,
                             verbose = FALSE))

sig_l <- fit$means[[grep("^sigma_", names(fit$means), value = TRUE)]]
sig_n <- exp(fit_n$means[[grep("^log_sigma_", names(fit_n$means), value = TRUE)]])
c(laplace = sig_l, nuts = sig_n, truth = 0.9)

The two backends agree on the variance, and the BLUPs agree across engines.

re_n <- ranef(fit_n)
cor(re$estimate, re_n$estimate)

A few random-effect specifications are NUTS-only. The Laplace path errors, with a pointer to NUTS, for: a single random effect shared across both the occupancy and detection predictors (share() semantics); a random effect combined with a spatial field in the same fit; and a random effect combined with visit-level detection covariates. In each case the deterministic path would have to fit something it cannot represent exactly, so it stops rather than silently fitting a different model. NUTS handles all three.

The reason for the boundary is in how the Laplace path works. The variance-component EM splits the random effects into an occupancy arm and a detection arm by which predictor they sit in, then fits each arm’s block separately while feeding its mode back into the other process. A single effect that has to be the same realization in both predictors breaks that split: there is no way to fit it once on the occupancy arm and once on the detection arm and call the two the same. Likewise the AGHQ debias works on a per-site marginal with the latent occupancy state integrated out in closed form; a spatial field or a per-visit detection design changes that marginal in a way the closed form does not cover. Rather than approximate silently, the validator stops and names NUTS, which samples the joint posterior directly and needs none of these closed forms. The cost is speed: a NUTS fit takes seconds where Laplace takes a fraction of one, and you read convergence from Rhat and effective sample size rather than trusting a mode.

Practical guidance

  • Want at least five to eight levels before the variance is informed. A random effect estimates the spread across levels. With two or three levels there is almost no information about that spread, the variance is badly determined, and a fixed effect that names each level is the honest choice. Five to eight levels is the rough floor where the variance starts to mean something; the recovery here used thirty and forty.
  • Use a fixed effect when the levels are few and each is interesting. Treatment arms, field protocols, a handful of named regions: these are fixed effects. You want their individual values, not their variance, and there are too few to estimate a variance well.
  • Keep at least ten or so observations per group for slopes. A random slope asks each group’s data to inform its own slope before shrinkage. Groups with two or three observations contribute almost nothing and the block leans entirely on the population estimate. Random intercepts tolerate sparser groups than random slopes do.
  • Trust the AGHQ default on small clusters. When per-group counts drop below about ten, the raw EM variance is attenuated; the default re.aghq = TRUE corrects it. Check fit$aghq$applied to confirm it ran. When it does not apply (split arms, crossed or nested groupings, RE dimension above 3), read the variance as a lower bound and refit under NUTS if the variance matters to your conclusion.
  • Reach for || when the correlation is not the point. The correlated block (1 + x | g) spends a parameter on the intercept-slope correlation, which is often weakly identified. If you have no use for that correlation, (x || g) drops it and estimates the two standard deviations more stably.
  • When not to use a random effect at all. If the grouping factor is the exposure you care about (the thing whose effect is your research question), it belongs in the fixed part of the model. A random effect is for nuisance structure you want to account for, not for the signal you came to measure.
